root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.name: Mammarenavirus choriomeningitidis

profile.headline: Globally distributed arenavirus of house mice; a neglected cause of aseptic meningitis and of severe congenital infection.
profile.syndrome: Biphasic influenza-like illness followed by aseptic meningitis or meningoencephalitis. Congenital infection causes hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intellectual disability, and is a frequently missed mimic of congenital toxoplasmosis and CMV. Transplant-transmitted infection is usually fatal.
profile.transmission: Inhalation or ingestion of aerosolised rodent excreta; vertical transmission; organ transplantation.
profile.reservoir: Mus musculus worldwide; pet rodents including hamsters and guinea pigs.
profile.diagnosis: CSF/serum IgM and IgG, RT-PCR; congenital cases need paired maternal-infant serology.
profile.prevention: Rodent control; counselling pregnant women about rodent exposure and pet rodents; donor screening after transplant-associated clusters.
evidence: Classic model organism virus with well-documented human meningitis, congenital syndrome and fatal transplant-transmitted clusters.

root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.name: Mammarenavirus lassaense

profile.headline: Rodent-borne arenavirus causing 100,000–300,000 infections and thousands of deaths annually in West Africa.
profile.syndrome: Insidious fever, sore throat, retrosternal pain, vomiting and diarrhoea; severe cases develop facial oedema, mucosal bleeding, shock and encephalopathy. Overall community case fatality ~1%, but 15–20% in hospitalised patients. Sensorineural deafness in up to a third of survivors is the hallmark sequela, and third-trimester infection carries very high fetal and maternal mortality.
profile.transmission: Exposure to urine or droppings of Mastomys natalensis (the natal multimammate mouse) through contaminated food, dust or rodent consumption; person-to-person and nosocomial transmission via body fluids.
profile.reservoir: Mastomys natalensis and related rodents, which are persistently and asymptomatically infected.
profile.geography: Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, Benin, Ghana, Mali, Togo.
profile.management: Supportive care with attention to fluid and electrolyte balance; intravenous ribavirin is widely used on the basis of older observational data now under re-evaluation.
profile.prevention: Rodent control, safe food storage, hospital infection control; vaccines are in clinical development (CEPI priority).
evidence: Continuous virologically confirmed seasonal epidemics with detailed cohort data from Nigeria and Sierra Leone.

geo.text: Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Liberia, Guinea, Benin, Ghana, Mali, Togo.

profile.headline: Cause of Argentine haemorrhagic fever; notable for an effective live-attenuated vaccine and proven immune plasma therapy.
profile.syndrome: Insidious fever, conjunctival injection, petechiae, thrombocytopenia and leukopenia; progression to haemorrhage, shock and neurological disease. Untreated case fatality 15–30%.
profile.transmission: Inhalation or contact with excreta of infected corn mice, especially during mechanised harvesting.
profile.management: Immune plasma given within 8 days of onset reduces mortality to below 1% — one of the clearest demonstrations of passive immunotherapy in viral disease.
profile.prevention: The live-attenuated Candid#1 vaccine, used in agricultural workers, has cut incidence dramatically.
evidence: Randomised and controlled studies of immune plasma and of Candid#1 vaccination give high-quality causal and interventional evidence.

refs.label: Protective efficacy of a live attenuated vaccine against Argentine hemorrhagic fever. AHF Study Group. J Infect Dis 1998
Treatment of Argentine hemorrhagic fever. Antiviral Res 2008

root/riboviria/orthornavirae/negarnaviri.baltimore_note: Ambisense: genes are encoded in both orientations on one segment. Conventionally placed in Group V, since the virion still has to supply its own polymerase.
